review:
I want to offer my sincerest and harshest admonishment to Paradox for discontinuing this game, then releasing the same exact game but with some extra UI updates and polish. 

It's highly exploitative and duplicitous. You've lost a customer.

16~ hours in, played through a couple missions, and I feel the need to write a quick review.

Like many others have said, this game has a load of potential to be absolutely awesome. I'm not complaining about figuring how everything works - I enjoy doing that. However, it is painfully obvious that the QA for this game was either non-existent, or done by a llama. 

complaints 

1. The most annoying thing by far is colonist job allocation. It's a horrendously tedious task to recount how many scientists you have every 20 minutes when one becomes a senior and messes with the equilibrium of jobs in your dome. Oh, wait, that's only for one dome. When you have 3-4 it is absolutely impossible to manage jobs until you get enough resources to efficiently specialize domes for specific specialists. However, it takes HOURS of absolutely mind-numbing micromanagement to get to this point. 

2. Please for the love of god let me queue up multiple actions with my rovers. The micromanaging makes surveying a pain. 

3. When setting up a trade route with the hauler, why can't the hauler auto-recharge its battery, and maintain the trade route...? That seems like common sense, because setting up the same exact trade route 15 times over the course of a game is fairly stupid. 

4. Why are all of the notifications the same size? Why am I reminded constantly that buildings aren't working, when they simply are full? Looking at you, concrete.

5. The map feels okay at first, but why does it minimize my colony overview whenever I open it?

6. Drone allocation is a paaaaai... just kidding. People keep bringing up drone allocation but the prefab buttons on the hubs make reallocating drones fairly easy

7. Was there QA for this game?

TLDR: Daaaaaaang the UI is bad. Some of the mechanics with colonists are also terrible. 

Positives?

Graphics are neat. 
The mysteries/missions are cool, story seems to progress at a decent pace as well. 
Building is very easy and straightforward once you play with it a little.
Resource management is always on your mind, which is something I like in base builder games.

Overall?

Most of the ideas behind the content is awesome, and the execution with many things is done very well, but then.. there's the UI. It honestly ruins the experience completely.

I'd recommend not to buy this game until they patch these issues, it's not worth the frustration.

Surviving Mars is an exccelent logistics based builder.
The problem with the game, and I believe that is the source of most negative reviews, is that it fails to communicate where the player focus should be at, and what is the main gameplay loop.

Examples:

- Multiple difficulty settings represented by the sponsors - the game is most enjoyable at it's hardest, because the main objective is to do your best with limited resources. If funding and resources are plentiful, there is no challenge to be had, and it becomes a grindy constant upwards curve. The game's name is SURVIVING mars.

- Colonist micromanagement - At first, when you build your first couple of domes, the ability to assign jobs and residences to colonists gives the impression that you should be micromanaging every little aspect of their lifes, and as the colony grows it becomes a nightmare. However, I quickly realized that it actually isn't vital to do so, just applying the correct filters to domes makes sure that the AI does a great job at moving citizens around, and (most of the time) they end up in the right place doing the right job. What seemed stressfull ends up being relaxed.

- Resource micromanagement - the game SHOULD make it very clear how much of a big deal Supply Shuttles are. Again, as with the colonists, the game starts by giving you the impression that you must handle cargo a certain way, with drones, depot positioning and even tedious manual assigned hauler vehicles. But again, once you realize how clever the Supply Shuttles are at ferrying every resource around when needed, it actually is a blast to see your little ant hill of a colony springing to life. Contrary to what many people are saying, the AI on this game is AMAZING, much better than in most colony management games. The problem is that the game fails in teaching the player HOW to use these tools from the get go.

This is a fun, addictive, stable and optimized experience that is getting an unfair amount of hate due to the (true) fact that it should communicate better what it's really about, and how to make the most of it.
But that is it's only fault. I reccomend it highly to any fan of city builders and space games in general.

There's a lot to like here, but there are some serious balancing issues with some of the breakthroughs that completely trivialize entire game mechanics. You'll spend almost as much time figuring out how to work around the AI quirks as taming the environment.  Terraforming the planet (if you get the DLC) feels really good, but takes so long you start to lose interest.

The much bigger problem with this game is that Paradox handed it over to a "game studio" whose entire experience was a few mobile ports, for the Below and Beyond DLC.  They screwed the game up super badly, to the point where it took months for them to get it back to a reasonably stable (bug-free) state.  This wouldn't have been a problem if it was contained to the DLC, but they "updated" the base game with most of the underlying code changes, which broke it for the people who didn't want the DLC as well.  Despite the uproar, Paradox refused to roll back the changes, or make the old version available for download, claiming it was "technically impossible".  Despite hundreds of games doing this with no problems at all.

Many of these bugs are still not fixed.  You'll be forced to rely on a couple of dedicated modders who have tried their best to fix most of these -- for free.  Paradox essentially screwed over a bunch of their customers and refused to back down when it looked like it was going to impact DLC sales.  So buy with caution.  it's a decent (if buggy) game, but you're also supporting an absolutely terrible publisher.

This is a painful review for me.  I LOVED this game until a couple of days ago.  It was my go-to game to unwind for months.  However, I knew when Paradox took over, there was a risk, and that risk was realized in the latest patch / dlc that is "Below and Beyond."  The re-balance is annoying.  The bugs are plentiful.  The mods are all broken.  This is far from something I'd recommend in its current state.

The real trick to this game is the game was okay.  Good, but not great.  The community mods added that final touch to make a great game, and it was working.  The clunky AI, fixed.  The lack of certain building types, fixed.  Now, all of these mods fail to work with the new version, and being an "older" game with an abysmal review score on the latest dlc, I do not see the mod community coming in to make the same fixes and updates this time around.  Without that community support, this game is dead on arrival.

I could be wrong.  The mods may come back and save the day, or Paradox may actually do some good and patch up their work.  But I doubt it.  I may check in a few months or a year from now to see if this has been addressed.  I may not.  Either way, Paradox has accomplished something no other game company has done.  This is my first negative steam review.  So, there's that.

The long and short of it is this.  If you want to see the ghost of a good game, this is the game for you.  If you want an actual good game, I'd look somewhere else.  I'm more than willing to change my review if these issues are addressed, but given the Paradox track record, I'm doubtful.  Even free, I wouldn't play this one in its current state.

EDIT 1: Still a fun game and still recommended. However I would like to be able to connect domes via tunnels as a proper way of moving people around and create Domes that interact with each other in more meaningful ways. As of now interaction is limited to Drones moving resources and Shuttles moving resources or people but only if they need relocate. It would be nice if Domes can help each other more directly, like a Science Dome connected to a Gaming Dome with some diners and grocers to fill the Scientists interests. And have those 2 connected to a mostly residential dome with lots of parks. We still have a dome ecosystem, but we can connect them to grow it even more. And if you want to have a solitary Dome that sustains itself you can still have that. 

================================

[h1]Colony Management: [/h1]

It is sad that the first few hours of the game left a bitter taste in people's mouths. I believe late game is where the fun is at in Surviving Mars but everyone's frustration with early game colonist management is not without merit 

When you first bring your colonists from earth you have a choice to pick Geologists, Medics, Security, etc. or just your Average Joe. Obviously everyone (myself included) thought it would make sense to pick colonists with job titles, they give a bonus to productivity when assigned to their respective jobs. [strike]However It won't take you long to realize that the game doesn't even give you simple interface to assign your colonists to their desired positions.[/strike]

It is possible to assign a colonist to a specific job or house without late game tech..

In the Hotkeys section bind
[list]
[*]Assign Job
[*]Assign Residence
[/list]
This literally solves the early game problem of getting your colonists to do the right jobs. No more Medics working at the tje factory nonsense or playing lottery High Priority setting on the info panel hoping that only the Geologist moves to the extractor and not the Geologis+Botanist.

The Dome system is designed to have a balance between  population, jobs and housing. When you build a new dome with 32 vacant jobs, you need to have least 32 residential slots so no one becomes homeless or unemployed when they move in.

When specializing your colonists, a late game bldg, the Mars University, automatically trains your regular colonists to fill specialized jobs your Colony needs. If you have 22 Engineering slots available in your entire colony, the Uni will train 22 Average Joes into Engineering Joes. I only build the University when I have Shuttles because your colonists will take a ride between domes, study, and then will fly back out to fill the correct jobs across your ENTIRE colony. Very neat. 

You can also isolate specific jobs to specific domes, via the Filter panel to create Engineering domes for Electronics, Biologist domes for farms, Scientists for research, etc. [strike]Maybe they should have disabled Specializations early game and have it unocked at the same tier ad the University...[/strike]

[h1]Replayability:[/h1]

During the (early) late game at around 100+ Sols, the game unlocked Mysteries which is supposed to be the story mode for your playthrough. These come in Easy, Normal and Difficulty mode based on your settings during game creation. I was only able to complete the 2nd step of my Easy mystery before the colony died to hunger and hypothermia.

I think the game revolves around the mid to late game Breakthrough's and Spires. There are different builds that you can use to get into the super late game depending on your RNG. I started a new Colony right after my 150 Sol Colony died and it s just not possible to play the same way you did before. 


[h1]Traits/Dome Filters/Spires[/h1]

These mostly go unnoticed unless you mouse over and read the tooltips to see what effects they have. If you choose to you can make very specific Domes to compliment traits to improve happnies. Hanging Garden Spire Biologist Farms with lots of parks is perfect for Hippies. Geologists like to Drink so it might be a good idea to mix them with Alcoholics and build a Spacebar to fulfill both's needs. You can Filter a Medium Dome for Unspecialized Colonists only, build a Shuttle, University and a Behavioral Treatment Spire and send out "Flaw"less Specialists to man your entire colony.

[h1]Different stages of the game imo[/h1]

- Early Game: Scan sectors, spam sensor towers, look for a "main base" for the mid game, try to survive (maintenance costs means you are on a timer) 
- Mid Game: Set up produciton lines, stock up, be at a surplus, build fail safes/redundancies in your power/air/water supply, be profitable (Rare Mineral deposits)
- Mid Game (Late): Build University/train colonists or specialize in uneducated colonists research, have a good shuttle/drone system
- Late game (Early): Build/research bigger Domes, have enough food and materials to sustain your pop/repair allyour buildings
-Late game (Mid): Mystery / Wonder 

I wasn't able to finish my Mystery. I tried to simultaneously build a Medium Dome while doing my Mystery requirements and my funding and repair materials ran out. First my Factories went down, followed by my Farms, Grocers, Diners, Refineries. Rockets we're grounded without fuel, without water, with broken drones and shuttles unable to resupply. Colonists got hungry and left the planet or stayed and froze to death or commited suicide. Survivors tried to run to the nearest dome but ran out of air along the way.

Pros

- Cute graphics
- Gameplay gets better the longer you play, challenging
- Fun Mid-Late game with plenty of replayability,  
- High tier unlocks (e.g. University, Sanotarium, Clone Factory, Resurrection) and other technologies that make your life easier (Shuttles <3)
- Combine your research/breakthroughs/spires and experiment with each dome
- Excited for mods/future additions. New services, textures, skins, darker nights, outdoor tourism, etc.
- Sense of pride and accomplishment when your Dome experiment comes through

Cons 

- No tutorial
- Ability to Assign Colonists to Jobs and Houses or Assign Drones to Hubs is hidden in the Hotkeys section
- Could use scroll highlight or an easier way to select mutliple drones
- Need more modules. Similar to how modders added a lot of goodies to Cities: Skylines
- Steep learning curve, plenty of information on the info panel but mouseover/tooltips can go unnoticed.
- Vewing at different angles is as smooth as using Google Earth. NEEDS a follow unit camera so you can take in the beautiful Martian view

[h1][i]Scanned the entire map. Is that it? Really??[/i][/h1]

I don't know what triggers the 2nd wave of research anomalies but in my playthrough it occured around Sol 100, I had just unlocked my Mystery quest, and had the entire map completely scanned. Suddenly Breakthroughs started popping up everywhere. I assumed this was the point where choose which way to "branch" out, aka decide what you want to build to get to the late game Wonder. 

There's a research that makes your colonists immune to suicide so you can put them in 24 hour slave-labor dome with people with the Religious trait and they'll never commit suicide from going insane.

I got a research that resurects colonists when they die. I went with this in my Sol 150+ playthrough with a Clone Factory Spire to make a Dome that works my clones to death, be resurrected, work, and die again. Hilarious.

Survival aspect is there, along with logistics, city planning, design, and resource management that comes with building games

GLAD THIS GAME WENT ON DEMO!! This is one time where the Steam reviews kept me from purchasing a game that I expect to really enjoy.  This has been on my list since it released in March.  No offense to the negative reviews, but to each their own.  For this genre, this is one of the best, most detailed and well thought out games I personally have seen.  I base this on the fact that my first such "sandbox" sci fi builder was on a 5.25" floppy disk on a bulky x86 machine (yes I am THAT old).

Some of the reviews - and I have read just about all of them - say it has no depth.  I disagree.  Details such ability to choose specialities and who shows up on Mars down to free ability(within reason) to place items within the game gives it as much detail as any similar game out there (I think I have them all).  

To the con side of things: Yes, I have found the build time to be a bit lengthy overall.  However, if this is your type of builder, then you are doing more than one thing at a time any way.  Could this be adjusted at the dev level?  Yes.  Also, I found the UI a little clunky, although in my opinion, its still fairly clean considering how many options are available in game.  One specific feedback is that infrastructure items such as pipes and cable could be separated.  As of yet, I have not found the ability to lay down multiple of the same item either.  Opportunities for improvement for sure.

Finally, I would say the biggest risk - and credit to some of the reviews on this - will be ongoing development and "value added" which I took into consideration as I made my purchase.  Its my expectation that the investment of the development to this point will be an indicator for an extended life of the game through additional DLC and game improvements.  

SUMMARY - I feel this purchase was a good value at its current price, and being able to step through the tutorial through a free weekend helped seal the deal.

Unfortunately i cannot say this is a good game.
From the beginning its always felt like it was missing some important mechanics, and i could never really put my finger on what. Every DLC partially fixed the issues, but i still could not figure out why this game bugged me so much despite how much i kept coming back to play it.
The Trains DLC finally made me realize the problem: theres no automation controls. A feature that ANY colony manager sim game uses, this one is missing. A feature that often gets overlooked, which is probably why i didnt even notice that was the main problem for so long, is missing from this game.

Why is that a big deal? There is no way to control where resources go on a macro scale. Local distribution isnt a problem because all drone hubs can reach the same depots, but once you start expanding outward you will find that almost all of your time will be keeping that remote area stockpiled with resources without completely draining another or having a lot of "dead" resources floating around that cannot be used due to how daisy-chaining depots works.

The game also has a bad habit of introducing mechanics that sound like you are supposed to be messing with them early on but either is impossible due to the insane upfront cost of resources or the upkeep for those buildings is so high it drains you super fast. The amount of times ive gotten a tech in the tier3-4 row that i cannot possibly use until several HOURS of gameplay later is baffling.

I dont know why this game is considered Very Positive reviewed. Every time i play this game i feel like i am struggling against the bugs and bad game designs rather than the game itself. Disasters never kill my colonies off, only slow them down. What kills my colonies is the fact that i cannot expand until i have a lot of resources, but i cant get a lot of resources until i expand. When i have a ton of roadblocks where my first thought is "how do i do that when the button i'd normally use in a game like this doesnt exist" theres a freaking problem.

If they added proper logistical/priority controls to depots and drone hubs i'd probably find a way around virtually every issue this game has. Unfortunately that lacking feature alone is the main reason i end up getting pissed off at this game at some point. Its funny because in games that does have it you dont even give it a passing thought

Apparently, I have over 575 hours in this game, so I guess I should review it.  I suppose you can guess that I enjoyed it and that it has re-playability.  They give you so many options and scenarios that you can play out that I am amazed at the depth of this game.  The game is both one where resource management is important and challenging at times without being so difficult that you feel like the game is work.  As far as colony-games, this is by far my favorite.  

Two points of advice on playing the game:  

You don't have to populate the planet right away.  Feel free to have some robots do a little resource building before sending actual humans to build your infrastructure just a bit.

Invest in buildings and technologies that require less ongoing maintenance, even if that means buying more expensive buildings.  The long term maintenance can be a choke point on development.  If you invest with that in mind from the beginning, you will find that you are more adaptable later in the game.

I preordered having watched many hours of YouTubers enjoying this game, and I have enjoyed it, but a lot of the 45 hours of play time I've clocked up was spent still watching YouTube while waiting for something to happen in-game. Huge periods are spent waiting for resources or research - there just isn't enough to do.

I've started three colonies and taken them through to completing the mystery. There's not enough variety in the rest of the game to make me want to start another colony. The randomised Breakthrough techs add the most interest - all the other techs are the same game to game but in a different order, while the selection of breakthroughs can cause you to tweak your play style somewhat. Not enough to make a significant difference though I found.

The dome management is limited to choosing which factory you want as each dome requires a large set of the same buildings to function properly (medical centre, grocer, diner, farm). There doesn't seem to be any way to get economies of scale, like a dome dedicated to farming for instance. This makes each dome very similar and not an interesting choice to set up.

One the plus side it's a fairly relaxing game and looks very good so as a colony builder it is good to pass the time for a while. It also takes a bit of time to learn the ins and outs of the production/maintence system to avoid shortages and colony problems.

It's a great game with a lot of potential, but at the moment it lacks content. There is no way to properly manage your population/drones/resources. The fact that you cannot expand domes or share buildings between domes is very annoying. Finally, there is no end game. The game feels 1 dimensional and is basically pointless by sol 150-200. More work needs to be done to make it a complete experience.

I hope that given further development time, or some really great mods I will change this to a Recommend, but as things are right now, Nope.  I wanted to like this game, I wanted to love this game.  Ultimately it fails in a number of different ways that have to be addressed before it becomes a really good game.

First, I'll give the credit where it is due:

1.  The visuals and the art design are wonderful.  A great amount of attention was given to landscape and dust effects and it shows.  The UI is clean and easy to read (though lacking in some extremely important areas).  Take the time to slow the game down and zoom all the way and really appreciate the beauty of the design.

2.  The base soundtrack is good.  Fitting for the game and not over-powering.  Voice acting is fine and sound effects are appropriate.  I'm not impressed with the other radio stations, but that may be an issue of taste.

3.  Game appears stable.  I've not experienced any major bugs or crashes.  Sadly, this should just be expected, but given the current state of game design, isn't.

4.  I am always grateful for any game developer that sets things up for modding support from the start. Opening your game up to the community is a great way to expand and develop in ways you may not have imagined, and fosters community.

Now, for my issues:

1.  The game is boring.  There just isn't anything to do, but sit around and wait for tech to happen.  It is really frustrating to hit a point pretty early in a game where I just walk away from my computer and watch a TV show or something.  There is a pretty simple standardized build pattern.  Make this, then this, then this, setup for this, make sure your drones are covering here.  Then bring in colonist and just walk away because it'll take a few hours to come up with another tech that you actually need/want in order to expand efficiently.  The only things that make one game different from another are location geography, randomized resource deposits, randomized tech tree, manufactured scarcity via disasters.  Other than that, every single game is exactly the same, and that same game is boring.

2.  Forced and manufactured scarcity.  The "difficulty" level of this game is based almost entirely about limiting what you have access to, which only means that you have to sit around longer waiting for an effeciency tech, or money to come in, or people to "respawn" on earth.  Again, back to point 1, now we're just sitting around being bored.  Increase meteor showers, more likely to have to repair things, using up non-renewable materials.  Increase dust storms, have times where you have to have built redundant power supplies or batteries, again using up resources but not actually challenging.

3.  Randomization for the sake of randomization.  I am not a fan of a randomized tech tree.  Especially, when so much of this game is based around managing scarcity, hiding a tech somewhere on a random tech tree that requires sitting around for an extended period of time waiting for research to finish to reveal the next random research is just frustrating.  Add to that unexplained random occurances (either because they are actually random, or a failure to explain a mechanic) like crop failures or a lack of anomalies anywhere you can get to without building tunnel systems and again the experience fails to satisfy.

4.  Inconsistent interactions.  Want to delete a building?  Okay, click on it and there is a button for that.  Have cables in a place you don't want them?  Well now you get to click all over it to try and find a "hub point" and then you may get the button.  It's a pain.  Want to send your Explorer and your RC commander to the same place?  Have fun micromanaging that the entire time, because you can't link them together or box select them.  Click on your explorer and zoom out to send them somewhere?  Great, make sure to zoom back in before you click on anything else, because hitting escape from the map view doesn't release the drone from your command like it does when zoomed in, it just opens a menu.

5.  A horrid lack of information for individual networks.  The game recommends, and the developers have recommended over and over to not build huge sprawling networks, because it is wasteful and requires more maintainence.  Great, then show us what supplies are available in each closed network.  Instead, all you get is a total power, total O2, total water.  You are required to click on every indivdual dome or outbuilding to try and find where something may be lacking.  Build a giant network and you atleast know what you are actually producing and using properly.  If I can't see, at a glance, the individual resource networks, there is no good way to actually manage it.  

6.  AI pathing and decision making is horrible.  Drones/Explorers are unable to handle terrain issues and wander off and get lost and out of power constantly.  Drones will get caught in loops of just moving the same resource from one stock pile to another.    Sometimes the AI remembers to use the tunnels, sometimes it tries to drive all the way around the map.  The colonists... well, they are just stupid.  Bring in a ship of botanists to work your new farm?  Okay, but two are going to be bartenders and one is going to be a researcher, while non-specialized people stay on your farm.

7.  Colonist needs management.  Again, another form of manufactured scarcity, but the mechanics don't make sense.  As you can't connect domes to each other (not sure why given the other things you can build) you have to provide the same exact sets of resources in every dome, just wasting space, building resources, and maintainance.  Since the colonists can move freely from one dome to another, there is zero reason why they don't walk or shuttle to the next dome when they want to go to the casino or bar.  If you can walk to the next dome over to work in an outbuilding (which they can), they should be able to use the service buildings in any dome just as easily.  Instead you are stuck, yet again waiting and hoping the random tech tree gives you a larger dome or needed upgrade.

All in all, I may have set this up to fail by wanting this to be good.  But I am hugely dissapointed in the product that has been delivered.  I have hope that future updates and mods will make things wonderful, and I think the game devs have setup a great framework to potentially create a fabulous game... but as it stands at this point, I won't recommend it to anyone.

So, this game is your standard tycoon game on mars.  While it is really cool seeing the first structures being built, after a few domes it becomes a rinse and repeat build process with disasters inbetween.

The game starts you off by picking your difficulty settings, which affects your "score", scenarios, and where you start on mars.  The Mars map is supposed to be accurate to the planet, but I still haven't found the face on Mars.  The map will indicate how many resources there are and possible weather conditions.  Once you pick the landing spot you are then taken to the regional map where the game is played.  

The regional map is divided up into around 100 sectors.  I can't remember the exact number.  You are given a scanned sector where you can land.  You also get some probes too for instant scans of the surrounding sectors.  Scans reveal resources, surface metals, and anomalies.   Scanning a sector before you land could lead to better starting locations.  Resources are broken down into concrete, water, metal, and precious metal/gold. 

Now you land.  Initially you start with a few worker drones, a mobile command drone, a transport drone, and pre-fabbed buildings.  You'll start off by setting up a command module, electricity, h2o generators, o2 generators, and a fuel factory, which you need for your rockets.  Once those are setup you'll build your first dome. 

Domes start small.  Eventually you'll research your way to medium, large, and XL domes.  Buildings inside of the domes are broken down into functions... living, agro, servicing, manufacturing.  There are also some external resource gathering buildings.  Domes monitor the needs and morale of your occupants and you can build based on those.

I got to give heads up to people reading previous reviews... A week or so ago they released a patch which made sharing domes between people possible via covered paths between them.  Before this, people would only move between domes for jobs and ocassionaly housing.  Now that you can connect them, you don't have to provide for ALL the needs in one dome, which was a godsend since your building area on the smaller domes was extremely tight!  Also, the pathways allow for a malfuntion free flow of o2, h2o, and electricity.  When I first got this game I lost half my colony because the pipe between domes busted.  Did I mention all the buildings have a "maintenance tax"?  Pipes and wires ocassionaly bust, but buildings have to be constanly maintained with resources or parts.

The game also has you constantly researching which allows for new buildings, upgrades, colonist perk, and Earth bonuses.  The research points are generated by dome buildings and a tiny bit from Earth sponsors, anomaly scans, and drone perk.  You can also buy research from Earth, but it was a function I don't think I ever used.  The number of points required for the next unlock are always increasing, so you'll have to build more research buildings as your colony expands.

Now that I've gotten most of the details out of the way, let me tell you why I think you should pass on this game... Mars is boring...  Mars is where FUN goes to die.  I think it might have gotten radiation poisoning on the rocket there and never made it.  This game felt like a grind to reach the end of each play through.  

After you build the first 3 or 4 domes, you'll realize there isn't a lot to this game.  Heres the quick rundown...  Build a dome, gather resources, build some stuff in your dome, make sure your people don't die, aaaaannnndddd repeat.

The domes are kind of marked off into triangular sections made up of the hexagon tiles, like...
...0
..00
.000
0000
Buildings come in small and large.  Smalls are 3 tile sized triangles and larges fill up the entire section.  There are also single tile parks and fountains to fill up the leftover tile or you can use it as one of the end points for your inter-dome paths.  

There's just not a lot of variety.  You'll find yourself building dome after dome just to keep up with the resource needs of the last dome you built.  Agro dome, then machinist dome, then electronics dome, then research dome, then agro dome, then machinist dome..... There's an analogy for this somewhere, like a snake eating its own tail... which it might end up feeling like when you notice you have a long daisy chain of domes, one connected to the next servicing the one before it.

In the end, I just didn't feel satisfied with this game.... Tropico, this is not.  

It has potential to be fun, but they need to add a lot more content.  Mars tourism needs massive expansion!  There should be hotels, clubs, other corps, a 3-tile sized bar, more than 1 building design... just a little more effort would've gone a long way!  The last patch did expand A LITTLE in terms of content.  I know if I was on this Mars colony I would've gotten tired of eating at the SAME diner 10 times over.  I think I know why some of the colonists commit suicide... it's just something different to do.

Update March 2021:

I replayed this game to see what the terraforming gameplay was about and was struck once again at how the game fails the genre.

The cornerstone of any colony builder is a simulation that works.  This is a game in which you can't trust the number that the simulation throws at you.  You can disable buildings, but the demand for their input doesn't go down.    You can see totals but you can't see a breakdown that shows where those totals come from.

For example, after being told that I had eliminated dust storms due to terraforming, I got an event that was a massive .. dust storm.. that was to last for three days and hilariously during that time my oxygen generators and atmospheric water generators no longer work.  I don't know who else has played this game, but if you can imagine not having oxygen generation for three days in a bubbled colony you can imagine that's just a flat game over.   An event that kills your colony.  You have to wonder who 'designs' that kind of thing.  

That's not challenging and it's not even amusing.  Worse, when something like this occurs and the player tries to take actions to survive and realizes that there are other bigger fundamental problems with the simulation it all sort of falls apart.

Compared to a game like Tropico where as you progress in the sim things get more complex and the challenges broaden, this game's main loop is an oversimplistic failure full of what feel like half implemented features.  You get rebels, and despite knowing who they are - can't do anything about them.  Can't arrest  them, can't hold them accountable for blowing up 60 people in a shuttle (it happened).  They just keep blowing up your buildings even after they become happy again.  Not only that, but there's no reason for them to be rebelling even in their character breakdowns. There's no way to address it and it just becomes a running gag.   It feels half-baked, like much of this game.

The end game is where things really start to fray.  Once you get a space elevator and mohole mine and start to wonder why you have to hold the mouse button down to fill your order up every time you buy 200 electronics.  How you now have 80 billion from selling gold but the game expects you to be buying and selling in tiny increments.  You have a colony that uses 2000 of a resource a day, but the NPCs want to trade with you in quantities of less than 50.  

It's clear that the early game was played, replayed and well tested and the end game - is just a mess of things that seem under-designed and under-implemented.

This game has many fine qualities and initially I had the just-one-more-turn experience I hoped for.

Mostly a well-made game but with a few serious flaws that makes the game tedious and boring. To keep this short(ish) I’ll focus on the things that doesn’t work:

Micromanagement needs to go. Colonists should swap jobs and residences instantly. No more having 10 unemployed geologists in one end of the dome and 2 mines filled with unspecialized workers in the other. No more having to fire and relocate the same unspecialized worker 29 times, before the specialist picks the job and residence. The game tries to be both a micromanagement and big perspective automanagement type of game but ends up being neither. The game should pick one direction and stick with it. If this is a micromanagement game, make proper controls for micromanagement. If this is a big perspective game, implement it properly and remove the need for micro.

Make proper overviews. When I go to the colonist page, I don’t go there to see how many gluttons I have in my research dome. I go there to see how many scientists I have and where they are working or living. Don’t force me to mouseover menuitems and click on every single colonist. Make proper filters so I can view multiple domes and multiple specialties at the same time, instead of traversing my 20 domes one at a times trying to remember the numbers of each of them. In a management game you need access to the information needed to manage the game. Removing this doesn’t make the game more entertaining. It makes it tedious and annoying to play.

Remove unnecessary features. Nobody uses “idiots” so why include them in the first place? Why do I have to delete a building, wait 5 seconds and the delete it again to remove it? And why do I have to delete cables in another way? Trim the game and make it to the point. All the unnecessary noise decreases the game experience. 

Add some challenges or some missions. An open-ended game with lots of micro is just a slow death. Add something that can give the player a sense of fulfillment. The option to create a wellworking colony without constant microing. Or something to achieve, like producing 500 rare metals in less than 50 years and stuff like that. Management game players likes things to “click” in place. We like to see things working and we like to complete something. Not just clicking back and forth to reassign workers misplaced by the game.

If these some og these things were fixed, it could be a great game. But as it is now it’s tedious. Kind of a shame, for everything else – sound, graphics, camera, (some of the) controls, setting/story - really works.

First thing, this game is addictive.  I shamefully admit that according to my stats and I spent just a few hours less playing this game the last two weeks than I have at my full time job.

Pros:
- The research tree is huge, which means the colony is evolving and changing for a long time.  Most of my game time has been spent on a single colony and I'm only about 2/3 through the research.
- The random encounters are fun and sometimes funny.  Usually the choices affect future game play.
- There are side story lines, in addition to the colony survival main event and the random encounters.
- The resource list is pretty big, and not only do some need to be crafted from others, there can be chains, such as crafting fuel which is in turn used to craft polymers.
- The colonists aren't cookie cutter.  In addition to age, gender and specialization, there are also perks, flaws and quirks, and those last really do influence game play.  Don't place the vegans in the same dome with the ranches.
- You aren't cookie cutter.  At the start of the game you can have randomly assigned or choose a commander profile.  That commander profile affects some of the choices in the random encounters.
- You don't get 100% recycling.  While that may seem like a drawback, 100% recycling in other games has been boring, and it really makes you strategize and be careful in your placement of buildings.
- It's not just the planet itself that's trying to kill you, your people can be their own worst enemy.  Suicide is possible for your colonists, and there's a reason you need a security force.
- While it is extra content, definitely get Green Planet and Project Laika.  Nothing like planning the steps for a future where your colonists mine and farm outside without their suits and without dying.  Plus, there is nothing cuter than seeing llamas and tortoises walking around in your domes, and you need Project Laika if you want to put your vegans in with the ranches.
- The graphics are beautiful.  If you are careful with your camera angles and zoom in completely, you can look through the windows and open doors to see interior details, such as dressers and closets in the living quarters.  You can't go inside buildings, but you can move through the tubes between domes.
- The drones are adorable when you zoom in on them.  They also look up to you and will miss you.

Cons:
- Micromanaging is a requirement, not an option.  Every time I get the colonists straight, I'll focus on nudging along resources or checking the mining and concrete production for just a little bit, check back on the colonists and at least some will have decided to do really stupid things, like move over one dome where there's no jobs instead of the dome one move in the opposite direction which does have jobs.  And sometimes they just won't go when manually directed until repeated commands and 5 or so minutes have passed.
- Your stupid micromanaged colonists will stay in a dome that you want to get them out of, despite removing all buildings and food in an attempt to nudge them into moving to better domes.  Trying to manually move around half of them, see 5 minute rule above.  Don't turn off the dome, they will stay in there and die of cold and thirst, rather than move to the dome just a few hexes away with residences, jobs and a diner.
- The mouse clicks are crazy.  Sometimes you need to left click.  Sometimes you need to right click.  There's really no logical layout, you have to just learn it, and while learning you are going to undo everything by clicking the wrong button several times.
- The developer did try to clarify the mouse clicks with the picture of a little mouse for many of the actions.  [u]BUT[/u], if you are left handed or are right handed but battling an injury, it will not reverse.  I think it will be a little harder for left handed folks, because the pictures did help me learn the clicks before the injury.  However even with that practice the pictures are screwing with my brain now.

9 thumbs up, but 1 thumbs down for the mouse pictures and the lack of logical layout in the mouse clicks.

Definitely get it on sale, since the season pass is pretty much required for this to feel like a full game, but if you can get everything for less than 30 bucks or so it's a pretty decent city/planet builder.  While it's fun, I have a hard time recommending it because the price is absolutely exorbitant unless you can catch it on sale. 

I wish Steam had a rating system rather than a binary yes/no.  I won't recommend it because the price is so high but it's a fun though limited builder that's worth putting on your wishlist and waiting for a deep discount.

Toilet flushing and rock hauling manager - Mars edition,

We will get back to the title shortly... SM has got amazing potential, but the game is hampered by a bunch of issues, let us have a look at a few; to give you, the prospective player, the flavour of playing this game. This is a small, small, sample.

1) No colonist management screen - colonists will choose jobs that they are untrained for then get suicidally depressed about it... The only way to fix it is to find the individual ant crawling on your screen and click on them. They will forget it next time you power down the building, get sad, and step out the air lock. (Just sacrifice specialisation bonuses atm and use generics till it gets fixed.)

2) On the topic of colonists, you travelled all the way to another Planet, and the only time you step outside the dome is to sprint from the rocket to the entrance when you first arrive? Why not just get thrown in prison instead? They could have the same experience of doing a s****y job and getting depressed (see 1) for much less effort.

3) The drones must be programmed with 1980s era Atari BASIC - they are that stupid. At this stage it's basically a stock pile manager, as you constantly move them around to make sure there is one nearby and your drones don't get stuck because they "forgot" about the pile of machinery on the other side of the dome. The more drones you have, the buggier the logic gets.

4) No way to move colonists between domes (so no specialised domes that work,) no way to easily automate resource transfer ... (You can kludge a system, but it's a bit ridiculous.)

5) By mid-game all the logic has broken down and you are micromanaging loo-paper transport!

6) GUI... oh the GUI... no shift click, no rubber banding, no grouping... Every problem in every strategy game UI, paradox made sure made it into this one. They must have been going for an achievment, I guess?

7) Oh, going back to drones, my pet peeve:. I get that hubs can extend range and increase maximum number; but, why do you have to assign individual drones to individual hubs!? FSM save you, should you have a stockpile with overlapping hubs (like a landing rocket, for example.) You will end up with drones stealing each other's materials, and getting stuck in a loop, with nothing getting done. Like I said - the mission programming their logic in 1980s BASIC is the only explanation.

8) Resource Harvesters generate waste material - cool, makes sense. But, their local storage can become full even if you have plenty of available dumping sites - because reasons... this results in drones randomly choosing to ignore the building from now on. The only way to "fix" the problem is to demolish it, and build again.

etc... etc...

I pre-purchased the game because it promised to be something that I've been searching for.  But, it's a gorgeous buggy mess that will make you claw at the flames, flames coming out of the side of your face. 

One more issue, the flavour content is mostly text box style - ok for 10$ game, not for one at this price point. However, some people might prefer that to a pre-rendered scene, so can't dingy it too much for that. It's a Paradox game after all.

Overall - buy if you are a fan of sci-fi and management games, BUT, you are getting an ALPHA level release. It's missing so many features that you expect in a modern sim that I, honestly, don't think it deserves BETA status. This is before we even mention the bugginess of the game logic. Luckily for Paradox, they don't show up early on; but, as the game progresses, and systems become more intertwined, it eventually throws its hands in the air and collapses in a steaming pile of broken logic. Then you can play toilet flushing and rock hauling manager - Mars edition.

If you don't have patience for all that, wait till it gets a few major updates under its belt, or is on a major sale. Personally, I really hope I can change this review to positive soon, this game promises to scratch so many itches... Paying full price for this mess has left a bitter taste in my mouth, if you are going to use your customers as alpha testers, at least compensate us for putting up with the BS. Not cool devs, not cool at all...

It's a casual city builder for space nerds. IT'S THE ONLY FICTIONAL WORK THAT SHOWS PEOPLE BOUNCING IN LOW MARS GRAVITY! It's super cool to build up several outposts of domes and to build up a fleet of reusable rockets that go back and forth to Earth.

But for how harsh surviving Mars should be, Surviving Mars is pretty casual. If you know how to balance resource production and make distributed rainy day stockpiles, you'll weather every disaster effortlessly. That is the totally 100% intentional artistic message, right? "Robots make Mars easy." Resources are a little too abundant, except for maybe colonists. Their mental breakdown mechanic of "renegades" is trivial to deal with. The diplomacy isn't the deepest, and it was pretty easy to destroying all rival colonies, if I wanted. They shrank the solar system to fun-sized, so the rockets make the round trip quickly enough to bail you out, instead of arriving with vital supplies only when everybody's dead. The biggest challenge is making your playthrough challenging, and any challenge you do find only really lasts through the early game. You're not making decisions of real consequence. I've done a few runs with hardly any deaths and zero colony failures. And yet, I still recommend this game.

There are a lot of event chain campaigns. They're fun. Since most of us aren't doing a dozen playthroughs, I would look up which ones are coolest and do those.

The Terraforming DLC adds a satisfying endgame. Somehow, a bunch of machines in one tiny village is enough to green all of Mars -- do the devs know how huge a planet is? Don't think too hard about it! It takes long enough that it still feels like a grand project. You do more than make percentage numbers go up: you take a barren planet, build a zillion terraforming machines, add lakes, and sow seeds. You are rewarded by a lush landscape of grass and trees, and finally, opening up the domes to the now hospitable sky. The second time around, it feels kind of tedious, until you try to make it as fast as possible by massively scaling up your operation.

If you want a deep and brutal city builder, play Frostpunk, Rimworld, or They Are Billions. If you're set on space, Oxygen Not Included has depth and personality, and your decisions can kill everybody. If you want to live the specific fantasy of a thriving Mars colony? It's pretty fun. And, somehow, replayable.

The game's not terrible, but not too good either. Buy it on sale or wait for some patches.

The amount of micromanagement is pretty infuriating and overall UI/UX experience is lacking for a simulation/strategy game:

Want to see the list of you colonists? It's not there. Oh, by the way, there are 2 renegades living in this dome. You want to find out who they are and see their details? Have fun randomly clicking at each colonist.

Want to select multiple units at the same time? Nope, you can't. Want to queue orders for a unit? Ha-ha, guess what -- nope, one order at a time.

"Trade routes" exist for transports, but they are extremely primitive: "take good X from point A and drop it off at point B", it can run multiple time until there's no more good X at point A or nowhere to store it at point B. After this the "trade route" stops executing. There are no quantity conditionals, not possible to set more than 2 points -- these aren't proper trade routes like in Anno games.

There's bunch of iron meteorites laying around -- of course the transport doesn't have an automated way of collecting those. Combine that with inability to queue orders and you get Meteorite Clicking Simulator 2018. 12/10.

Work assignments are seemingly random. My geologists are farming and my botanists are digging for minerals outside, because that's how AI assigns them ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ It is possible to assign a colonist to a specific workplace manually, but this assignment isn't permanent (and as I've already mentioned there's no list of colonists).

I'm not sure what's the reason for those issues -- rushed to capitalize on recent Space X craze? UI limitations because of console versions?

Anyway, enough with the rambling. The game has potential but needs a lot of more work.

I really really really want to love Surviving Mars... The concept is great, there are some interesting mechanics that you don't see in other building games, there's some sense of randomness about it.  But, it's absolutely not worth the price tag in it's current itteration.  If you're reading this review, perhaps the game will be in a more flushed out, stable state by the end of 2018.  Lets do a deep dive.

First and foremost, the world generation process is truly random at times.  The nuance and problem with this is that you may find yourself reloading a generated world multiple times in order to ensure that you have a supply of things required that make the early-game playable.  Of course, if you're a new player, you won't realize how screwed you are until about 5 hours into the map.

The UI is severely lacking.  From what I've read, it's due to the intent of the game being released across multiple platforms, but what we're left is a shoddy UI.  There's no ability to select an idle worker, there's no ability to view all colonists from a single spreadsheet-esque view to micromanage.  The intent is that the built-in-algorithms are going to 'optimize' things anyway, so players don't need to do it.  Although, then I went to a building and saw a lazy worker working in a job that he was specialized in, providing 0 skill points towards productivity.  

The 'random' meteor hits, geysers, etc... are truly random.  The problem with this is that it incredibly breaks the continuity of the game.  If we can accomplish cross-planet colonization, we can't get a little advanced notice when a meteor is about to take out our dome?  Nobody thought ahead to any early-warning systems?  I think back to platforming type games where there's a big difference between punishing someone with randomness, versus expertise in being able to adjust to a situation.  This is not skills or reactions, this is just random punishment, and a horrible way to design a game.

Don't misunderstand, there's a lot to love in this game with the colony building process, expansion, resource gathering, base optimizations, etc... However, it is not currently worth the price tag.  It is an Early Access game with a lot of promise.  I would wait until this game goes on sale at half price, or wait until it's in a more flushed out state before investing into it.

Underwhelming - this is the word that comes to mind once you've spent some time in Surviving Mars.
It's less surviving mars as surviving the tedious and combersome methods that aren't provided for managing your colonists, especially as this is a colony management / city-building type title. 

Trying to get your colonists into the jobs that they are most suited for in order to garner the best bonuses and keep them happy is immensely frustrating; and honestly it begs the question how the design decision was made to forgo more robust colonist management tools. (And no, these gameplay issues should not be relegated to be solved by the modding community).

Each colonist has their own special traits, and jobs, etc, but nowhere can you see a list of these colonists in these categories or manage them accordingly. The domes allow for some granularity when controlling who lives in them, but at the end of the day you need most if not all of the same services in every dome in order to maximise their comfort and happiness; so why bother, each dome is practically a colony onto itself at that point as attempting anything more specialised is simply pure mind numbing tedium. 

"Researching" technologies feels unimpactful and something that just runs in the background with no real reason to specialise or pursue particular technologies. Scanning territories is precisely the same process, once again, just zoom-out click a square and move on, very little Incentivisation is utilised for this mechanic.

All in all the feeling this title leaves you with is simply one of frustrating boredom, because it should be good but it's just not. There are plenty of other titles out there that do either city-building or colony management far more comprehensively, unfortunately (and with sincere disappoinment) Surviving Mars doesn't really measure up in either of these categories with enough gusto to make it special.

Surviving Mars lets you manage a human colony on Mars from the laying of its foundations; the life support systems and habitats, to actually landing the first colonists. Expanding and growing the colony until it becomes a fully self-sustaining metropolis with always a room for expansion.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
From your early beginnings to a huge bustling self-sustaining metropolis, careful planning and execution is required. It is so you don't take too long or run out of resources. You start off with one ship landing with a bunch of drones and resources to use. As opposed to every other colony survival games that start you with a number of colonists already, there are no colonists at start; you need to build the foundation for your future colony first. That means the power, water, food, oxygen, and fuel infrastructure has to be built first to support the future inhabitants. This adds a bit of tension when your first settlers arrive and finally set foot on Mars. Their survival completely depends on your initial infrastructure. You can also request additional supplies from Earth in exchange for money and land more colonists as long as you can prove to Earthlings that your newly found colony is very capable.

The tech tree is partially randomized, so you probably won't get the same set of techs twice. It discourages min-maxing and allows for a more dynamic tech progression. Surviving Mars also doesn't give you all the available techs in one game, meaning you might need to play a couple of games to see them all.

Surviving Mars offers you a variety of buildings and structures to build your colony until it slowly becomes self-sustaining, comfortable, and even start to earn funding instead of spending them to request supplies from Earth. Again with the dynamic tech tree, there is less min-maxing and more on dynamic gameplay progression. As a result there is no best way to play this game, it all depends on what techs are given to you and what you want to prioritize; with the ultimate goal of having a huge self-sufficient colony with lots of drones helping it. Although once you get to learn the know-hows, it might feel a bit repetitive on your next playthroughs, despite the variations in your approaches.

The colony simulation/survival aspect is well thought of, it closely resembles Cities Skylines, with each individual having their own simulation. You can track them as they go along with their daily lives, working as a scientist, shopping for groceries, and going home to sleep and relax. They have their own wants and needs; affecting their performance and their desire to either stay on mars or go home. Despite lacking the complexity and depth of other similar titles, the balancing of critical life support systems and resources becomes its own logistics mini-game and in my opinion mimics the feeling of managing a real off-world colony. It really felt like I was sustaining the people, it was natural enough and never felt like a chore.

Surviving Mars gives you a plethora of choices when starting off a new colony. The whole planet of Mars is available for you to play on, divided into hex grids with each hex tile an area to play. Every hex has their own varying environmental conditions and concentration of resources. Some will have more metal or concrete ores, others will have more water. Some go through too much sand storms while other tiles experience a lot of meteor storms. Picking a relatively quiet tile with lots of resources are recommended for everyone, while those looking for a challenge can pick the more chaotic and scarce tiles. There are also different options for you to choose from to really customize your starting conditions, offering a bit of replayability and customization for the game. There is also enough endgame content in the form of tech breakthroughs and various anomalys you can research and study.

[h1]Technical Analysis[/h1]
Surviving Mars runs surprisingly smooth on my system(i7-8700k, 16GB RAM, GTX 1080) compared to other CPU heavy strategy titles such as Cities Skylines or Civilization V. Even with heavily populated cities it still ran at very high frame rates. There's no performance issues or crashes that I've encountered even when playing at long stretches.

The graphics and visuals are impressive, I always find myself pausing the game and going to photo mode, to take screenshots of my huge metropolis against the backdrop of a beautiful Mars landscape. The addition of a photo mode is commendable, with all the adjustable lighting, day/night cycle, and atmospheric conditions. I also loved how they made great effort in the sound department, offering a masterpiece of over 5 hours of music. With three in-game radio stations plus an official game soundtrack. Its more than you could ever ask for.

[h1]Value[/h1]
For the fun and challenging gameplay along with its initial start customization, dynamic progression, and enough endgame content; I'd say Surviving Mars is worth it in its current price. Advisable to get it on a sale since it goes on sale often. My only gripe is that some of the additional content is locked behind the Colony Design Set (supposedly just a skin pack) and the Expansion Space Race.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Surviving Mars is a fun and challenging game that will most likely satisfy your offworld colony survival and city building desires, just don't expect too much depth and complexity from it.
