After reading all the negative reviews I was not sure if I should pick this game up for quite a long time. After having played a bit I do not fully understand why so many people are complaining about it. Yes, it is repetitive, as almost any city builder is. Yes, the micromanagment is sometimes annoying, but this too is part of the process of building stuff. As a comparison: in Cities Skylines (also from Paradox Interactive) 90% of what you do is checking on your godforsaken traffic and compared to that this game is relatively harmless. I agree with some people, that somewhat more content would be preferable and that UI and colonist AI is in need of some tweaking. Yet I can fully recommend this game for anyone who liked Planetbase and Cities Skylines. It brings a very cool approach to the whole colonising-a-new-planet-simulator and is really enjoyable.

This game is really cool but my one gripe, and it really pisses me off, is that electrical power "leaks" out of broken cables.... what in the actual fuck, when have you ever heard of that. When a cable breaks then power just stops flowing, the electrons don't start fucking leaking out of the wires.

The colonists have different personality traits, but they do not have relationships and those traits barely affect the colony. The vast majority of the colony's work is done by rovers and their drones, all of which require pretty dull micromanagement. And then there's the weird controls: map scrolling is slow, ALT triggers the camera movement and is inversed by default, rotating objects is R and T and not the perfectly normal Q and E, and there are a bunch of regular functions that do not have hotkeys or the availability for them to be assigned.

I had a different experience than others with the difficulty. I chose the US start on an average map and it's been painfully easy. If you double up or triple up on storage, no meteor or dust storm will abate your colony's growth. What's got me writing this negative review so early on, only 6 hours or so, is because it really does seem like the build up takes quite a while, that the payoff can't be that great, and the colonies just cannot have the diversity of a Cities: Skylines city. Most of what your'e doing is by necessity, and I have had the poor luck of not having any dome beyond the basic one after having over 100 colonists already. Even if I had, I wouldn't be too impressed by the way my city looks.

The first update should be free; it should involve rover/drone overhaul, providing deeper relationship mechanics for colonists, and making the controls/camera/interface standard like most other games have them (this is so clunky).
This game is not complete; it should NOT have dlc for a good six months or so.

I think this is a good game when all is said and done.

The foundation of what is there is really solid. If it has flaws, I think they're mostly in conveying ideas to the player. I haven't yet found any systems that didn't work, but the way you organize colonists between domes and the way the domes themselves are self contained I think might not be obvious to people.

The tools the game gives you to assign people to specific domes are actually quite powerful and well automated, but the game relies on you setting up fairly specialized domes for your colonists to really get the most out of it, and a lot of the progression in the game ties to building bigger domes which you can put more buildings in which lets you really max out your specialization and devote more space to the actual purpose of the dome rather than just keeping people alive. The starter domes ARE too small to put everything you want into, and that's part of the point, I think. Once you get medium domes the game really lets you start building specialist districts for your colony and really start producing stuff. But you shouldn't try to put every building in every dome, especially not at the start. People won't be 100% happy all the time and that's fine, they don't need to be, you just need to keep in the black as far as sanity and health goes and try to keep your comfort up as best as possible. Your colonists will muddle through until you get established and can start building specialized domes, that's part of your goal in surviving, to get to that point, and you've got to make decisions about how you want to use the limited space you've got in your domes.

A lot of people have posted complaints about the colonist management system and the fact that people will work jobs they aren't specialized for, and to that I would have to say that they will do this if you don't provide colonists with the correct specialization in that particular dome, but this is very easy to do because you can set preferences per-dome to choose who should live there, and the game will quickly rehome people to meet these. You should have things like a manufacturing dome full of engineers, a mining dome with geologists, a farming dome with botanists, and these specializations also affect the kind of comfort buildings you will want to build because each specialization has preferences for recreation. You can even do things like making a retirement dome or a medical dome where all your old people go when they can't work any more to get them out of the worker housing, or a dome where people with flaws go to get cured and then leave when they no longer have those flaws. You can specialize domes in childcare by moving your children over there and giivng them buildings to get them educated and give them specialist skills, and the game WILL automatically handle all of that for you just by using the preference system. I really think people are just not understanding how the system works because I find it works very well, while still requiring you to make sure you have a good supply of colonists. It's powerful but you need to make sure you feed it enough people and skills for it to really shine, and with people and skills being an important resource in the game, that's a good thing, i think.

The same is true for resource management, the game actually can and will automate a lot of it for you once you unlock shuttles (or pick the option to start with them) and you can also do a lot of it by placing your storage depots centrally and overlapping your drone coverage over them. You don't have to do much micromanagement at all really if you set them up right to start with. The only micromanagement I've had to do is when I wanted to send a rover to harvest surface deposits, that I think could be improved a bit by having a "scavenge area" command that is a bit wider ranged, or letting drones treat the transport like a mobile stockpile. But for the actual colony itself the drones are very good at getting stuff where it needs to go, but make sure you have enough of them, if you don't have enough drones it's like running out of teamsters in Tropico, you'll stall.

If I have one complaint with the game it's that it's perhaps a little easy? I completed it with no real issues at 450% difficulty. I think it really is a matter of understanding how the systems in the game interact. But I still recommend it because I think this is absolutely the kind of thing that modding would be well suited to expanding on, adding more, longer term goals and challenges depending on what kind of game you like. At the moment much of the difficulty is front loaded, when you're first setting up a colony it's a real juggling act to keep everything running and supplied, but once you get established it gets a lot easier. And the game sets its goals to get around this because you're scored on how quickly and effectively you can achieve your mission objective, so you're pushed to expand quickly and get set up as fast as you can, but if you like playing the game just to play around with the mechanics, you may find the later stages a little trivial, though I'm still playing it to see how big a colony I can build.

The random tech progression is also a bit odd in that some things can be really trivialized by the time you get them. Like I don't actually need a fusion reactor because I rolled all the technologies to make half a dozen wind turbines produce more power than it does without any staffing and with less maintenence. In a way it has that typical Haemimont tendency to kind of falter in the endgame, a lot like Tropico 5 actually. The early stage is much harder than the later one though they've tried to add the Mystery thing to give you an end game. I think though that the size you can build colonies to would be better served by having some more mission goals past the first 100 days and also some things that require way more people involved to make them work. You can honestly win a hard start with just a couple of domes and less than 100 people but the game supports way more than that. it just relies on you really being self directed in building bigger.

If you do decide to get this, play it on as difficult of an embark as you can because that early game is really the best bit, figuring out how to set up a working colony I think is where the game works best and if you fail a bunch you can try again. If you're on the fence about whether you want to get it, I think maybe wait a while and see what mods come out for it because the game has put a good bit of work into supporting them and I think they could make this game shine the same way they do in Cities Skylines. The foundation here is very promising and most of the criticism I could level at the game is really just that the mechanics it has are sometimes underutilized by the pacing and challenge level of the later game. If it could keep the scarcity and need to expand into new territory to survive, I think this would be the best colony sim I've played in a very long time. As it is, it's still a good game and I've had fun playing it for the time I've put in so far.

I really hope the game gets picked up by more people and some mods are developed to build on the core mechanics more, and I'd love to come back to it at that point to play more.

This is gonna be a lengthy one so sit back or skip to TL;DR.

It's fun for the first few hours, then you realize you've seen it all. It's a shame there isn't any other proper game set in colonizing and industrializing a planet/moon (Planetbase doesn't count, it's even more barebones than this). Let me elaborate a little.

Let's start off with positives!

-The aesthetics are nice and it is fun observing the colony live off its life. Every time I look into a dome and watch for a moment I see something new going on, a colonist doing a morning exercise in a garden, or elevators go up and down as workshifts begin and end. The attention to detail is incredible and the colony really feels like a living, breathing system.

-The game also runs really well at least on my system, to the point where in the first time of my gaming career I've had to forcefully limit the FPS so that my GPU won't whine as it's pulling 700fps...

-I love love love the ability to screen applicants to send off to mars to make the red dream a reality. It makes it feel as if every colonist is an individual with their own strengths and weaknesses. You get to feel like NASA, ESA or whatever picking the cream of the crop!

-I also love the fact that the research tree is randomized every time so the challenges you face are always new and it adds to replayability.

There's seeming depth in the sense that you get to decide working hours and which kind of crop rotation to use.

On the surface, the game is incredible. It plays to its strengths and sticks to it.

But onwards to negatives:

On the deep end, the game is surprisingly lackluster. The research is unlocked by scanning anomalies... which is not really surviving mars, it's pulling tech out of thin air and it gives access to some insane unlocks that make the game feel unbalanced on several occasions as it can completely take the challenge away from "surviving" mars. 

One thing I hate is that food never goes bad so you can stockpile massive amounts easily...

Colonists are specialized or nonspecialized in their certain fields, but they seemingly hate their choices and you see scientists working in mines, or engineers in farms despite having much work in their own fields. It gets tedious babysitting them especially in the earlier game where you really need to squeeze all the available manpower you can get to reach self sustainability... After which the game runs itself and your space utopia only has you stuffing domes wherever they fit and that's the extent of that... until the mystery kicks in at around 100 sols or so. They offer interesting challenges and storylines, but since the part of surviving mars is done and in the past, the incentive to continue begins to diminish rather quickly.

Don't get me wrong, the mysteries are a nice addon and offer extra challenge and unpredictableness, but once you learn what each is, they quickly lose their worth, especially if you're going after score attack, which means you need to pick certain location which is always the same, same mysteries, and same sponsor/commander which makes hardest difficulties always be the same diluting some of the variance in the later playthroughs. It kills off one variant of the gameplay styles real fast.

One thing I also wish there was: There aren't any colony wide edicts to push in case of running out of resources, I would imagine rationing, energy conservation etc to be a thing, afterall these are trained people getting sent to mars to establish the first ever colony yet they whine and moan as soon as they can't get to the nearest pub for a pint... Stellaris did this well by having a harmonious empire produce specific points that you could use to push edicts to save yourself or to advance yourself, but only momentarily.

TL;DR Surviving mars has tremendous potential, but right after reaching self sufficiency fairly early on, it quickly loses its touch, there is very little to do, and even in the early period you are mainly just babysitting your colonists so that they don't run from their workplace to work in the wrong field...  It is still fun to play and try things out, but after one playthrough you kinda feel like you've seen it all, no matter the mysteries. If the devs don't incorporate new buildings and mechanics, I'm afraid it's once again down to modders to save a game from dying an untimely death.

PS: Surviving Moon overhaul please!

Surviving Mars is at its best when you are building a base organically in a reactive fashion dealing with your immediate needs combined with the events the game throws at you. I had a ton of fun with my first three colonies in that regard. Just enough complexity and depth to be a pleasant, engaging distraction.

Once you reach the point where you have mastered the mechanics and can easily create a sustainable colony, the only challenge remaining is to fill the map. Unfortunately the graphical repetition and moderate system depth makes this an unappealing prospect.

I would definitely not start this game by trying to min/max it or reading a bunch of guides; there isn't enough depth for that. A "perfect" playstyle leads to stale gameplay, but bootstrapping a struggling colony when you are first learning everything is plenty of fun and well worth the price.

The fun in Surviving Mars is found in the challenge.

At its heart, Surviving Mars is a resource management game. In that sense, it is less like Cities: Skyline and more like the Anno series. Like islands in Anno, the most effective way to play Surviving Mars is to specialize the living domes to maximize the overall resource output of the colony. The big difference though is that any break in the supply line, or any lack of redundancy, can literally lead to the death of your colonists. Oh, you weren't prepared for that Dust Storm? Well, tough luck.

As an example, during an event triggered by one of the many "mysteries" of the game, I once had one meteor destroy a tunnel I couldn't afford to repair. In a day, two thirds (200 people!) of my colony asphyxiated. Yet, I did not give up and found a way to soldier on with those who survived. Recovering from this disaster to have a thriving colony once more was extremely rewarding! And those brave, unfortunate souls will never be forgotten.   

Some reviews suggest that the game becomes boring after a dozen hours. This wasn't my experience at all. During my first playthrough, which lasted about 20 hours, I was absolutely enthralled by the game and at no point was I bored. I suspect these reviewers played on one of the "easier" difficulties (i.e., choosing a sponsor with lots of resources and a relatively safe location). This is actually the default setup for the game when you first launch it. 

While growing your colony using one of the "easy" difficulties can be fun for a while, it doesn't take long before there's no more risk apart from overpopulation. Without any external challenge, it's relatively easy to have a pretty healthy colony that can run on autopilot.  

In comparison, choosing a sponsor with more challenging traits, like that weird fertility cult, brings a whole new dimension to the game. If you also choose a location where death *literally* rains from the sky, then it becomes a truly rewarding experience not only to survive, but to make your colonists thrive on Mars! 

With that said, there are quite a few points to criticize. The UI looks great, but there are some functionalities which are not clearly explained. This means that it might take a long time before a player discovers, if they do at all, a UI functionality which improves their game experience. Additionally, while the AI is relatively robust, there are some features which are surprisingly missing. Among others, rovers can't be automated to transfer resources between depots (which shuttles do just fine, but require a tech unlock). Also, there is no easy way to allow colonists to transfer between domes apart from shuttles. 

Most of the issues with the game can be easily improved on with patches and possibly future DLC. Since Surviving Mars is published by Paradox, I have no doubt that they will provide significant post-launch support; in fact the development team at Haemimont Games has already begun addressing some of the feedback they received at launch.

Surviving Mars is a wonderful game filled with wonder and potential! I would recommend it to anyone who likes the sci-fi setting of Mars and resource management games like Anno. 

My advice: challenge yourself, and the game will reward you for it.

Update: As I expecte, the series of free updates and DLCs has shown the willingness of Haemimont games to improve their game steadily. The addition of many features requested by the players, such as rover automation and tunnels between domes, has already improved the gameplay significantly.

Ambitious, fun, sophisticated, beautiful, engaging, deep, challenging. It is a step up from your other colony management games and really something we have been waiting for years without knowing it. There are some fairly big negatives but the positives seem to far outweigh the challenges, and the game clearly punches above the usual Paradox line.

I was building a new home for humanity on a cold, lifeless rock as the International Mars Mission. The food was almost never a problem, but boy... did we face a couple of challenges in other areas, from constant resource shortages to mental health issues to dome migration problems, you name it. For a good part of 90 hours we somehow survived, until we hit a very bad situation with metals and the life support systems started failing in the entire colony. Some hard decisions could still be made, not everyone would have understood them... but in the end, I decided to start over with Japan as the new sponsor. Very different capabilities from the IMM. I'm loving this faction so far, the early phase is making sound progress as a 100% unmanned mission. With my lessons learned from the Colony #1 which at times was utter hell, the experience has been quite serene and enjoyable so far.

The reviews have lots of complaints about colonist management, but the majority of those seem to be a misunderstandings of the game. Impatient perfectionists will be ruined with this game - there is lots of hair pulling early on, and a couple of things which are not very intuitive with the game. Then you get smart and start to READ UP. I can't really see how you'd enjoy the game without, unless you select a lot of crutches to make it just too plain easy. There are mechanisms to handle many of the big and small problems, but also this game is a lot about macromanagement, you should also tackle the big picture and not get hung over every small detail.

The developer also seems to have moved on, and there likely won't be new DLC. But they left a trail of 19 months of patches and upgrades behind them - the game feels pretty complete and many things are now polished to be very playable. Modding is well enabled in multiple areas and is likely to bring the game forward in years to come.

So what does the game have to offer? Some of the positives:

+MUCH more challenge than in Cities: Skylines, whether you are looking for just the fresh or the pure masochistic

+Friends of industry/economy/logistics management games will be glued to the screen for hours and hours. There's really a fair bit to see here and it takes a while to get a good grip of the structure.

+Several layers of automation vs decisions you can make at both micro and macro level

+There is a decent, stable player community

+Modding scene is active and the current selection of mods can really enhance the game, addressing many quality of life issues, bringing new buildings and gameplay, or adjusting your favourite nuisances in balance and difficulty

+Mods work smooth and really enhance the game (I slapped on 80 mods for the second game and so far, they work fine...)

+The game experience is highly configurable even in the vanilla version, for replayability. Many sides of a good sandbox game are there. 

+Different sponsors, landing locations, game rules etc. require very different survival strategies and a new level of resourcefulness from the commander.

+Besides the juicy and robust colony simulation, there is some additional spice to the game in terms of diplomacy, trade, LOTS of different disasters, special events etc.

+The phases of the colony are varied and interesting, from unmanned exploration and preparations to the first manned landing, the early survival, the later management of a large colony and eventual terraforming of the planet

+Colonist management is an important part of the game and does a good job. It reminds you of other excellent titles in the area - at least Rimworld and Star Traders: Frontiers come to mind - and there is lots of personality and possibilities with the colonist traits and interests. Most of the times you will be more concerned about the macro level of specialization, sanity, comfort, morale, and of course having the right number of workers in all the right places.

+Resources make a very meaningful hierarchy. Start from producing the basics and don't dream of being an electronics mogul when all you have is 50 pioneers trying to keep the water supply running and survive to see the next morning. You need water before you can produce fuel, fuel is needed for polymers... Fail to grasp and cherish this aspect of the economy and your colony will be in ruin before long.

+The tech tree has a randomization model which is simple and highly workable. It's basically linear but you don't know the exact time a certain technology will be available. There are a few interdependencies too, and breakthrough tech, modded tech, or just configurable game rules also break off the linearity, too.

+The domes are a really unique aspect to the game. You'll add your very personal touch with your design, ie. what buildings you will put in the dome for each purpose, whether it's advanced industry or a retirement resort - and you'll probably fine tune your designs for a long time to come. Dome sizes also evolve as your colony grows.

+Overall, many mechanics are innovative and really bring out the hardships and challenges of living on a barren, remote planet. Being self-sufficient is a big challenge early on, you are dependent on the rockets coming from Earth, but you are supposed to send something back too...

They have done a solid job with this one.

Space. Survival. City building. All in one. A good casual game that doesn't require the relentless attention as games such as Cities Skylines or Jurassic World Evolution (2). It feels far more laid back than that, at least on Easy difficulty.

Positives:
+very replayable
+meaningful tutorial that helps you discover the games complexities
+cool details like mars dust on items and wear qualities in buildings

Negatives:
-my god this soundtrack
-who designed this UI, the year 1999?
-needs more things to build
-path to survival feels too linear

Overall, if this game is on sale, it's totally worth a buy. Of the four colony/city building games I've purchased during the most recent base-building Steam sale, this was the one I actually kept coming back to.
Refund this game completely and I will consider the relaunch. But I will not pay you twice for the same game you lazy bastards.

Pros:
-The early game, mid game, and end game all have their share of unique challenges and mysteries.
-A variety of sponsers and mysteries makes for a lot of replayability.
-The mysteries come with some very engaging narative.  I won't give any spoilers, but the writers went all out on these.
-It's the most realistic portrayal of Mars colonizaton I have ever seen and it's generally very believable.
-The random events and event chains are very well written, they present very interesting choices and help immerse you in the world.  10/10, would have one of my own domes go rouge again.

As of the release of the Green Planet DLC, I have actually been able to move some of my biggest cons into the pros category.  Knowing Paradox, you can be sure they won't stop there.

Notes:
Surviving Mars can be a bit slow at times, which I'm fine with because I enjoy a good relaxing game that I can play while listening to a podcast or music. Having a background playing Banished, it really helped with the learning curve.
There is lots to do on this little red planet in so little time.

For those considering purchasing this game, this word soup is for you:

The first epidemic you'll face is the age of lazy welfare sucking seniors. Non-contributing members of the harsh Martian colonisation effort. In this game, seniors do not work; ergo, they do not contribute to the efforts. They leech your resources, and take up valuable real estate that could otherwise be occupied by fertile, sexy, rizzed up Martians. Let me save you hours of time and a few re-do's: I realised that suffocating the seniors in their own dome was so much easier, more efficient, economically friendly, and ultimately (after like 5 failed attempts) sent me into a rapture of satisfaction; feeding them and supplying them with housing, water, food, and oxygen became an option - Finally! this game started to really open up for me! *wipes evil tear*
I mean....You could go the [arguably] slightly less extreme route and actually feed them, and keep them alive (yawn). But ultimately, you'll want to isolate the seniors in their own domes and keep them away from your valuable housing vacancies in your working domes so your vigorous, youthful Martians can get to slappin' cheeks! ;)

The second epidemic you'll face will be resource management. You will probably learn how to deal with this issue long before your seniors start terrorising your casino's on bingo nights. But keep in mind that resources like water never stop extracting, so managing how much you pull out of the ground versus what you can store and save versus what you cyclically use should contrast with when to turn your factories and machines on and off to save valuable power and resources. This becomes especially important as you scale the difficulties and select landing sites on Mars that are more resource scarce than other locations. (Helpful tip for beginners: If you want the most resource rich location on Mars to start your first colony, use coordinates 4S112E at the selection screen)

I recommend you max out research in your Physics, Engineering, Biotech, Social, and Robotics trees BEFORE you invest any Science into the Terraforming, or Recon & Expansion trees. UNLESS your plan is to mine asteroids, or delve into the underground early, then maybe dump some brainpower into Recon & Expansion. Terraforming is late game grunt work, I wouldn't worry about this until your colony has stabilised a little bit and you've got a comfortable groove set in.
On the topic of Science. OUTSOURCE!!!! this is the best use of your capital. The better tech you get the easier the game becomes. Use your money to outsource whenever you have the funds. The early techs are as inexpensive as 1000 Science each, but the late game techs are tens of thousands of Science per selection; be wise with how you spend this currency, it costs time, not just science. Establishing a solid foundation for research is fundamental to developing a successful colony. Research labs, and Hawking Institutes will form the bulk of your Science department for most of the game, however if you're struggling early on getting science, it might be worth it to dip your toes into the Recon & Expansion tree to get the Recon Centres - They can seek out discoveries in the cosmos (as well as discover resource rich asteroids) to give you a couple thousand extra science from time to time.

Be very picky of your first 12 founding colonists. Don't accept mediocre. You want the Sexy, and Workaholic traits if you can get them, and get an even number of males to females (obviously). Your Earthling Martians need to be Hard working and DTF!!!! The idea is to get off the proverbial nipple, and build a regenerative colony. And NOTHING regenerates like sexy, hardworking Space Cowboys! Yeehaw!

Use the time selection to your advantage. Being able to pause and speed up the game is extremely useful when trying to manage the clock. Your spacebar is your friend!

Build domes that work for your colony and you. I know it sounds like a great idea, but don't build the "Las Vegas Dome" where all your colonists can just go kick it and have a fun weekend. Outfitting it with a few casino's, a wonderful place where your colonists can go watch the rocket launches, and get f'd up at the Space Bar during the all day cocktail hours - This is a waste of valuable resources and real estate (go ahead, ask me how I know this). Your colonists are not community college frat boys looking for a good time. They're FORMER community college frat boys looking for a good time, who just so happen to be on a sponsored suicide mission to the Big Dead Red - We need them SHARP and PRODUCTIVE! Bare in mind when assembling the guts of your domes; your essential kit is Housing, Infirmary, Grocery, Diner, and a fountain/pond, you might need an Electronics Store to satisfy some gaming needs that might be a requirement of some colonists, but for the most part this is the bare minimum to maintain sanity to a level that encourages reproduction. I recommend building a separate dome exclusively for the freshly born Martian crotch-goblins and have this outfitted with nursery's, schools, and playgrounds. This will keep the children out of your "fertile" domes [aka they wont be taking up housing vacancies in domes where you need as many occupants "busting the bed springs" as possible.]

The martian rail lines are very useful for accessing remote areas from your main populous. I use this for getting resources trapped in deplorable areas of the map. I have had issues with salvaging/deleting rail lines and stations in a few games, and in others, they delete just fine. So they're moody - great...

All in all, I like this better than Banished. I wish there was more content in the workshop, but honestly, I don't think the game needs it.

Good luck and Godspeed everyone!

I find this game super relaxing, even though its a survival game. I just sit there, cultivating my crop of colonists and drones until around sol 100 which is a good six-eight hours of game play, and then I start a new game with a different sponsor/mystery etc. The game is beautiful, has a lot of complexity to learn but isn't too crazy despite its initial appearances, and there is a lot of variety both in the techs available each game, disasters/map characteristics, and of course in its crazy amount of DLC. Do what I did and play a game, get some more DLC, play another game with the new DLC repeat, rather than getting it all at once.

Disappointed.
1. It's not a citybuilder, as the assets are too few and it's therefore repetitive if you play it as such.
2. It's not an economy builder, as the resources similarly lack variety.
3. It's not a sim, as the colonists require micro-management and then often later disobey your instructions.
4. The tools for this micro-management are also limited: you can't, for example, tell your vehicles to go do this and then do that in a sequential fashion.
5. The camera that this forces you to use is clunky (not to mention the UI).
6. Whilst the tech tree is randomised, and thus offers the potential for infinite replayability, the foregoing give each playthrough a feeling of sameness, as you'll still go through the same building-limited-infrastructure/mining-same-resources loop.
For example, I want to build a colony entirely out of AI; with a bit of luck on the tech tree this is possible, but it makes building domes pointless and crucially means you're not going to have any ability to shape the personaliity of the colony as you will with colonists and spires. So, you think, can I build with AI only and then populate with biorobots? Again, a big roll of the dice is needed with the tech tree, but say you do get Extractor AI and the Positronic Brain, you'll still need colonists to build them.
It's just my opinion, but the tech tree needs to have more meaningful strategic choices and less randomness. This might then succeed in giving SM an end-game: presently you reach a point where you've done all the research and accumulated all the population/money/resources and are just left with nothing more to do. I'm sure community mods will introduce more diversity in buildings and resources, and I might revisit (I have already), but for now two playthroughs have been enough (and it's still enough after the Opportunity Update patch). Still disappointed.

I love this game so my "do not recommend" comes from a place of sincere and sad frustration. Long story short: the game is broken as it currently exists. 

There is something bugged with the terraforming which means you can sink HOURS into the game only to find out later on that your game file is simply broken and that you can't complete the terraforming process. I even submitted a support ticket only to be told that my files were corrupted and that I should ask the community for help. It seems a bit backwards for the company that developed/owns this to volunteer free labour from the community to fix your game. 

[b]I've had this issue in multiple new files of the game[/b], which has quite frankly broken my trust. [b]I simply can't recommend it as it currently stands.[/b] 

It is such a shame because the game itself is amazing. It's complex, has great replay value in the challenges and profile types. But to replay it you have to be able to play it in the first place...

Surviving Mars is a city builder by the same people who gave us Cities: Skylines. It's polished, and shiny, and easy to get into. It's also a hell of a lot of fun, though not without its faults.

You'll spend most of your time juggling various resources, designing your colony, and trying to keep everyone alive, even though they seem determined to kill themselves at the drop of a hat.  I get that life under a dome would be hard, but killing yourself because you can't find a diner to eat at seems a little extreme.

The game is also MUCH better with the Green Mars DLC. I would go so far as to say that you shouldn't bother getting the game at all unless you planned on buying the Green Mars DLC. It *makes* the game at this point.  Without it, you'll run out of things to achieve far too early... so factor in the additional price with your decision to purchase.

In terms of gameplay... Early Game is outstanding. It can be tense,and fraught with peril and frustration, before you even get your colonists.  Sorting out your early game manufacture and structure is a lot of fun.   Mid-game, when you're also juggling the needs of your population is more laid-back, but you need to juggle employment and housing as well as resources.  It's also when your randomly selected storyline, or 'mystery' kicks in... and you're worried about toxic rains, storms, and meteors.

Late game, after you've got a few 'wonders' built... well, it turns into a bit of a grind. You're not struggling at all, but there's a lot of waiting around before you hit your next milestone or 'win' the game. There are no more toxic rains or storms or meteors, and you're playing a waiting game.

Late game needs more work. A lot.  It doesn't spoil the game, but you need SOMETHING to be doing while you're waiting for numbers to tick over, or for research to complete. Maybe a 'second tier' mystery/story would be a welcome addition.

This game is well designed, with countless hours of playtime.  It reminds me of old Outpost 2, or what Outpost 2 would have evolved into.  The radio stations playing in the background immerse you into what a not-so-distant Martian world could be like.

There are a few bugs still in the game, mostly contained in the Below and Beyond DLC.  They are rare, and usually crash the game, but they are still present.  The updates of this game have been deafly silent for a few years now.

The game play itself is engaging, keeping you coming back for more.  The mechanics of the game work pretty well, even though sometimes the mechanics do not behave as you intend them to.

I paid real money for this game and now they have taken it away and ask me to pay again for an upgrade which I do not want. I want to play the game I originally paid for. Completely unethical, downright insane.

I'm going to start start out with what this game is lacking, which is a significant list unfortunately...

-Little to no tutorial
     I feel like this may have been by design.  First colony on mars, no one to hold your hand because no one has done it before right?  I'm actually (mostly) okay with it.  It's a steep learning curve but, made the game more fun and challenging as a result.  That being said, managing colonists is a pretty much a crapshoot till you get the hang of it.  I spend several days not understanding why they never did what I wanted until I realized that there was an "apply" thing you had to click when specializing domes which wasn't explained and was unique to that menue so I missed it early on.  

-Colonist(people) not as advertised
     Early gameplay videos put emphasis on the people's induvidual needs.  This really isn't a thing, as most of them share needs that can be met with a few basic buildings.  They put a lot of thought into the perks, flaws and quirks of the colonists but this part really fell flat as they don't matter much in the long run.  You DO technically have a lot of conrol over them and can fine tune to a point, but it ulimately doesn't really make a huge difference in terms of game progression.  Job/dome assignments get thrown out the window the second you raise priority in another dome or basically do anything else.  In the end, once you gain access to a few relevant techs, you won't bother and in late game all you are really doing is just trying to keep up with the f***ers who seem to have no concept of birth control whatsoever.

-Mid to endgame content
     Seeing this in pretty much every review.  It's hard to find a reason to keep playing beyond a certian point.  Once you've moved past the basic needs of starting your colony, there isn't much to do.  Each mission DOES come with a quest/story and these can be fun and unique.  (there is even one that offers a bit of combat and defense building!)  But you've pretty much played it out well before the sol 200 mark.  They could really use bigger maps, more resources, other factions.  Basically anything else to do on the map... you're giving a HUGE map the basically has a couple good building areas and 4 basic resources (Water, concrete, metal and rare metal) and you can complete most of the objectives even on a diffecult game without out bulding on more then 20% of the map.  Only reason to explore at all is to find anomolies to scan to unlock new techs.

Despite all that, I'm still somewhat tenatively receommending this game because:

-The radio stations
     They will get repetative, but no more then your average pop FM station (and the songs are game unique... so no Taylor  Swift!)  The catchy music got me over a few of the mundane humps of the game.  Best one is free earth radio imo!

-Map and starting diffuculy
     You can crank up the disasters and play with frequent meteors, dust stroms and cold waves for a decent challenge.  Then play with a tougher sponser for even more challenge and ability to replay.  But again, once you've made it over the hump it's all the same.

-Story/quest
     A few unique ones, I've done 3 and loved them, but they are still mostly secondary to just getting established.

-Tech tree is random!
     This is a cool feature.  Makes for an added twist on each playthrough.  Trying to survive a map with high meteors without the mds laser, or cold waves without the subsurface heater can be really challenging.  

-Mod support.
     Call them lazy programmers, but at least they opened it up for community content.  Might be the one thing that really saves this game.

Bottom line...
     I'm not sure I'd pay the full 40 bucks for this again if I had the chance, but it's still quite fun, hoping for more content and mods to save the day.  It fills a niche somewhere between simcity, the sims, planetbase and tropica.

As much as I'd hate to do it.  I cannot recommend this game.  At the surface it looks like a complex, intriguing city/colony builder and planner.  But within 5-10 hours of playing, you realize just how shallow and lacking in content this game is.  By hour 20 (in my case), I was losing the motivation to continue playing.  Between the lack of micromanagment, simplistic drone/resource management AI, painful resource "level-gating", and overall lack of general fludiity and flow, the game is just bland and poorly executed.

The resource requirements and upkeep costs to advancing are the game biggest enemy.  You want your colony to be efficient, self-reliant, with a sense of autonomy.  But there isn't any.  The frequent breakdowns, the starved and skattered resources with only one-to-two methods of collecting them, and the poor colonist job AI makes the game tough, but in a hair pulling frustrating way.  There are times where one system will have a fault, and it will completely cripple and unhinge your entire operation.

A lot needs to be changed and implented to this game for me to provide it a positive review.  However, at this time, I feel safe to make the assumption that the game should've been early access until all the systems were more fleshed out.  I'll update this review depending on changes.  But at this time (3/28/2018), I cannot recommend it.

The colonization mission in [b][i]Surviving Mars[/i][/b] does not start as you expect with a handful of colonists, but mainly with drones. With a few large rockets you land on the big red planet and you first have to arrange some basic facilities before you can even think about taking people to Mars. For this you allow several rockets to fly full of materials and even prefabricated buildings.

The idea is that you build and control a city, just like in other [i]Paradox[/i] games, but with hardly any water, oxygen or any materials at all.

This interaction between Mars and Earth means that you have to deal differently with the expansion of your colony. You have to think further ahead than with the average builder. When you have a cargo machine parts flying in to build new windmills, you have to make sure that you have enough for both building and maintaining it. It can take a while before you have enough money to get a new transport. This makes you very dependent and gives a very isolated feeling. If you make wrong estimates, you can get totally stuck or your settlers go through a period of hunger with death as a result.

The in-game graphics are 3D with a manual camera, and the engine is capable of producing some very lovely images. Camera maximum zoom is fantastic, enabling you to see your friendly drone ‘faces’. The day-night cycle includes the sun moving across the sky in a realistic manner, casting shadows of varying intensity and length, and reflected convincingly in the glassy domes.
Buildings and units are all very nicely modelled and animated, with some very creative internal dome structures taking advantage of the reduced gravity. Human colonists look good too.

There are four radio channels with wildly varying instrumental tracks between them. Sound effects are appropriate and professionally implemented.

With no proper tutorial and only a handful of useful in-game hints, [b][i]Surviving Mars[/i][/b] can be quite hard to get into in the first few gaming hours.

For fans of city builders / colony simulations, it should offer many, many hours of enjoyment. For those who don’t like the genre, [b][i]Surviving Mars[/i][/b] is not going to change your mind.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Plenty of things to keep you busy
- Good research trees
- Unpredictable colonists
- Easy to become invested in your colony
- Great visuals and performance
- Huge amount of buildings and customization

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Not much of a toturial
- UI and controls could be polished and improved

[h1]9/10[/h1]

The early game is great, but having bought all the DLCs, the late game gets tedious, especially when it comes to terraforming. It feels like the game gets to a stage where you are just trying to complete it for the sake of completing it. It feels so unrewarding. There is no incentive to build huge cities either or expand more than you really have to. Talk about setting up a Mars colony and there's no incentive to go over a few hundred citizens. 
A lot of the mechanics of the game are a bit silly as well like the fact that when you get leaks or damaged wiring, there is no way to automatically shut off affected areas if you even have taken the time to put in valves and switches. Waste of resources ultimately. You would have thought there would be safety features on a colony whereby planning for redundancy would have been imperative. The drones are a bit of a mess too with their highly limited ranges and inability to move through control zones, instead, being relegated to serve up to a set distance from their hub. SEEDS have to be the worst if you have bushes and want to put them on a rocket. Forget those several thousand units of seeds stacked up next to the rocket. Your drones will instead go and pick up fractions of seeds of the bushes to fill the rockets up.

Maybe the game is worth it on sale with huge discounts, but it just doesn't feel like there is that much longevity unless you are the city-builder type that just wants to make the surface of Mars look pretty. Even the modders can't fix this game.

Fun and relatively simple colony sim that could have used a little more polish. 

The good.
-the OST is amazing
-slow paced chill experience
-satisfying tech tree with pretty OP and fun upgrades in the late game.
-excellent progression from pinching penny's  and barely filling housing to raking in billions and overpopulation being the main problem in your colony. 
-well written story cards and interesting and rewarding “mystery events”.
-very customizable game options and tons of variety in random events and starting settings that can have pretty big impacts on your early and mid game strategies. 
-environment design is gorgeous. Still looks great at macro scales in 2025.
-has a lot of character and S O U L. You can tell the devs cared and had fun making this game. 
-its overall a really fun game with a lot of replayability if you like slower paced games. The progression is very rewarding and well balanced. Challenging but not unfair. Different challenges and goals present themselves as you progress and watching lakes fill and tundras transition to forests is very satisfying. My complaints are mostly centered on the very late game so don’t let them discourage you from playing this (you should) (and get the Green Mars DLC. It’s vital). Mods also fix most of my gripes. 


The bad
-buggy.
-the game ender (in the very late game, don’t worry) is that colonists and drones start having trouble managing themselves. Colonists lose the ability to efficiently distribute themselves and there isn’t an efficient way to do it manually so keeping homelessness and unemployment in check becomes a Sisyphean task. Drones also struggle to build things and will sit idle despite there being ample resources in nearby caches. Sounds like a major problem but this only really becomes an issue in your colony in the very late game. You’ll have forests and thousands of colonists before this really becomes unwieldy. Theres a mod for this that has helped in the past but is out of date as of 4/2025.
-not enough building variety in the late game. Once you are fully teched and self sufficient, you end up just building the same buildings over and over in every dome in order to keep everyone employed. So. Many. TV Stations. 
-art design. The domes look great and most of the building designs are nice or at least totally fine. However there’s a few buildings that are so bad they impact the overall aesthetic. The garish Nurseries, playgrounds, and amusement parks are the worst offenders. 
-missing some basic UI and control functions that should be standard in a colony sim with rts elements like this. You can’t double click or shift click units to select all similar types, only some units can set up transport routes (dozers can’t automate waste rock transport wtf), you can’t issue complex orders to more than one transport at a time, unless a unit is pinned, it can be very easy to misplace it then all you can do is scan the landscape playing where’s Waldo until you find it, no mini map which would solve a lot of the issues with the camera and losing units, not a great queue or prioritization system for building and giving orders. Mods fix a lot of these issues.
-the camera is odd. It zooms out a fair amount but not as much as I’d like before transitioning to an overhead map that’s on a fixed camera angle. Theres a bit of a delay in this transition and the default scroll speed is pretty slow so scrolling across the map becomes tedious. A mini map would really help this. There is a minimap mod but I haven’t tried it.
-mostly complete slop DLC. I mentioned the OST is excellent, it is. The other radio stations aren’t so don’t bother with any of those. Cosmetics you can take or leave. Get em on sale I guess. I haven’t tried the trains or underground DLCs but from watching YouTube videos I’m not really interested in them or what they add to the game (they’re also buggy as hell apparently). The only totally vital DLC I’d get is the green planet one. This unlocks a whole tech tree and the terraforming mechanics. Honestly should be part of the base game but ya know, devs gotta get their bag. The in dome buildings is also worth it and project laika is fine. The rest is probably not worth it unless in an on-sale bundle with other stuff. 
-once you are mostly terraformed, the lighting gets obnoxiously bright and saturated simulating a healthy atmosphere and clear sunny day I guess? I like the idea of a warmer lighting at this point in the game but it was not implemented well and it overexposes things to the point of losing detail in highlights. The nights are also a bit too dark. A mod kind of fixes this but it just preserves the way days looked prior to terraforming so you don’t get a new lighting effect as you progress. 

Nitpicky complaints. I give this a 7/10. Worth a play if you’re a genera fan.

It would appear they have invested a great deal of time and effort into the mechanics and resources of this game, i.e they created a great platform. Sadly they skimped on creating content for that platform.
The game is fairly hard to a point, and when/if you overcome the initial struggle, all of a sudden you find yourself with no reason to continue. One would think that if there is no written content or challenges, they would have opted for a more sandboxy approach, but there is none. Once your colony run smoothly your only reason to continue would be to finish all research and duplicate your builds over and over to go bigger and bigger. but theres no incentive to do that.
In short, this game needs nor only more content, but a rework on the gameplay itself, in order to continously incentivise expanding.
